extracted.intended_audience: law students and patent practitioners (readers studying U.S. patentable subject matter doctrine)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and applying U.S. § 101 patent-eligibility principles (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) as articulated in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit case law, with emphasis on biotechnology and software/business-method contexts. Uses cases such as Myriad, Mayo, Chakrabarty, Funk Brothers, Athena, Vanda, and Bilski to illustrate standards and tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws-of-nature / natural phenomena / abstract ideas exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable (the Patent Act contains an important implicit exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are 'the basic tools of scientific and technological work' that lie beyond patent protection because patents that tie up their use could inhibit future innovation. Courts must apply this exclusion in a way that avoids eviscerating patent law (i.e., recognize the exception but not so broadly as to exclude all inventions that embody or use natural principles). (See Mayo; Diamond v. Chakrabarty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature rule for naturally occurring DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: A naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated from the rest of the genome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation alone (severing covalent bonds to extract a gene) does not render the gene patentable if the claimed subject matter is essentially the naturally occurring genetic information (Myriad Genetics). The court emphasized that Myriad did not create or alter the genetic information encoded in the BRCA genes; discovery alone is insufficient under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA distinctness / synthetic-created-molecule rule
rubrics_metrics.description: cDNA (complementary DNA) is patent eligible because it is not naturally occurring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: cDNA is created in the lab from mRNA and yields an exons-only molecule not found in nature; therefore it is not a 'product of nature' and is patent-eligible under §101, except that very short series of DNA with no introns removed may be indistinguishable from natural DNA. (Myriad opinion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery alone does not satisfy §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Groundbreaking, innovative, or brilliant discovery does not by itself satisfy the §101 inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court in Funk Brothers and Myriad emphasized that finding or discovering a natural phenomenon (e.g., the location/sequence of a gene) does not make the phenomenon a 'new and useful composition of matter' eligible for patent protection; invention requires more than mere discovery of what exists in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chakrabarty 'markedly different characteristics' test for patentable manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A product is patentable if it is a nonnaturally occurring manufacture or composition of matter with 'markedly different characteristics from any found in nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty held that a genetically modified bacterium with new capacities (to degrade oil) was patentable because it had distinctive name, character, and use differing from natural organisms. Apply this when the claimed subject is materially altered from natural counterparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims' form matters: information-focused vs chemical-composition-focused claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims expressed in terms of genetic information (the informational content of DNA) are different from claims expressed in terms of chemical composition; the former may render isolation insufficient for patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim focuses on the information encoded in DNA rather than on a novel chemical composition, courts will scrutinize whether the claim effectively covers the natural phenomenon itself. Myriad's claims focused on genetic information, undermining the argument that chemical changes from isolation made the claimed molecules patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical alteration/severing bonds is relevant but not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Severing covalent bonds (chemical alteration) when isolating DNA may be considered but is not necessarily sufficient to render the isolated material patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit judges disagreed: some treated chemical alteration (cleaving covalent bonds) as creating a new molecule and thus dispositive; others rejected bond-breaking as 'magic' that creates a new product. Courts will analyze both the structural/chemical differences and whether claims depend on those differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of natural laws may be patent eligible (distinguish claiming law vs applying it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a natural cause and well-known means of observing it is not eligible, but claiming a new treatment or application that uses a natural law is not the same as claiming the natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court distinguished claims that merely encompass a natural law from claims to new treatments or applications that use that law (citing Vanda: method of treatment by administering drug at certain dosages based on genotype was not directed to a natural law). Evaluate whether the claim is directed to the law itself or to a novel practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step / inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Mayo, after identifying a law of nature, courts look for an 'inventive concept'—an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent on the natural law itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim recites a natural law plus only conventional, routine, or well-understood steps, it may fail §101. Courts ask whether the additional claim elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO past practice and reliance interests are not dispositive for §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office's historical practice of granting certain patents and patent holders' reliance interests do not control the judicial §101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court gave little weight to PTO practice or reliance interests where statutory interpretation and constitutional principles were at issue, and noted that Congress had not clearly endorsed the PTO's gene-patenting position (Myriad). Government positions in litigation also affect deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test is not the sole test for process patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test (tie to a particular machine or transformation of an article) is not the exclusive test to determine whether a claimed process is patent-eligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski rejected the machine-or-transformation test as the sole test; courts should use it as a useful clue but not as definitive. Process claims must still be analyzed for whether they claim an abstract idea, natural law, or application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas, business methods, and software: computer implementation is not a magic wand
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning an abstract idea or algorithm into a computer-implemented process ('by means of a computer') does not automatically make it patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have resisted allowing mere recitation of computer implementation to transubstantiate an abstract idea into patentable subject matter; claims must add something significantly more than the abstract idea itself (Bilski discussion; critique of Federal Circuit practice). Also consider novelty/obviousness separate bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let patents 'tie up' basic tools of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents should not be granted in ways that 'tie up' the use of basic scientific tools or impede the flow of information necessary for future innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating §101, courts consider the social cost of granting exclusive rights over fundamental principles or discoveries and weigh that against the incentives patents are meant to provide. Overly broad subject-matter grants are disfavored.
